newsitem.title: UK: Commodities enter November looking vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: Commodities enter November looking vulnerable.

text.p: Commodity prices mostly opened November looking vulnerable after late October sell-offs in gold, oil and grains and new volatility in industrial metals.
Speculative money preferred the more lucrative returns to be found in equity and bond markets as various factors eroded confidence that commodities were a strong bet at present.

Oil was sold heavily in New York and London on Thursday as investment funds took the view that the benchmark Brent Blend of crude was unlikely to return quickly to a $25.06 post-Gulf War peak of two weeks ago.
"The bulls have taken a serious blow," said analyst Charles Gray at brokerage Prudential Bache.

Blunting the rally on oil were statistics showing that low U.S. stocks of heating fuel were now beginning to rebuild, although they remain well below normal for the time of year and few analysts expected crude to slip quickly back below $20.
Elsewhere in commodity markets gold has dropped $5.00 in a week and is holding precariously above key support at $375 an ounce. It closed in London on Friday at $377.65.
Low U.S. inflation robbed bullion of allure, nor was it helped by fears that European Union nations may sell gold from reserves to raise cash to meet monetary union debt criteria.

Further news of subsidised European exports hit wheat prices on the Chicago Board of Trade on Thursday and near-month December futures fell to trade just above $3.70 per bushel by Friday's mid-session.
Bumper 1996 crops have sent wheat sliding from a historic high at $7.50 which it touched in March at a time when drought in several regions had eroded world food stocks to 20-year lows.
The world price of copper stabilised to end the week on the London Metal Exchange (LME) just below $1,960 per tonne after a rebound from a Tuesday sell-off that saw it as low as $1,916.
It had rallied above $2,000 on Monday. But dealers said that positive supply-demand fundamentals seemed to be encouraging buying of copper.
But rallies were being sold in to, perhaps by banks that took on a hoard of copper built up by Yasuo Hamanaka, the disgraced Sumitomo Corp dealer and have not yet fully sold it.
Hamanaka built up a big long position before he was fired in June as an alleged rogue trader.
Funds did buy zinc, however, on trader talk that financier George Soros had upped his stake in that metal.
Sugare saw a sharp technical sell-off during the week and coffee and cocoa struggled to make gains.
